study.title: Psalm 67 The blessing of God for Israel and the nations
study.overview: Psalm 67 is a community prayer that connects the blessing received by God's people to the mission of making the name, the way and salvation of God known among all nations. The psalm begins by asking for divine mercy and favor, passes to the desire that the peoples praise the Lord for their justice and government, and ends with hope of abundance, continuous blessing and universal reverence. The logic of the text is clear: when God blesses his people, this blessing becomes public witness to his character and draws the nations to praise.

outline.title: Blessing that reveals the way of God
outline.explanation: The psalmist asks for mercy, blessing, and the glow of God's face upon the people. The goal is not only internal comfort, but that the way of God be known on earth and its salvation reaches all nations.

outline.title: Nations called to praise
outline.explanation: The text repeats the invitation that the peoples praise the Lord, because he judges with equity and guides the nations on earth. The righteousness of God does not turn away the peoples; it invites them to rejoice and worship him.

outline.title: Fruit, prosperity and universal fear
outline.explanation: The earth responds with fruit and God continues to bless his people. The final result is that all the ends of the earth recognize and fear the Lord.

study.context: The notes provided describe the psalm as a public and community prayer. Matthew Henry understands him as a psalm facing the church, with a horizon of expansion of God's people between Jews and Gentiles. Adam Clarke also reads it as a prayer for the expansion of the kingdom of God and, in his introduction, mentions the possibility of having been written after Babylonian exile; this dating, however, is only an interpretative hypothesis and cannot be affirmed with certainty from the text itself. The title indicates liturgical use, with string instrument, reinforcing its character of congregational song.
study.theology: The psalm unites three central themes. First, God's blessing upon his people is grace, not human merit: mercy, favor and presence are requests as gift. Second, Israel's election has a missionary purpose; the blessed people make visible the way of God for the nations to know their salvation. Third, the government of God is just and universal: he judges with equity, leads the peoples and deserves praise from all. The psalm also associates spiritual blessing and material provision, for the fertility of the earth is a sign of divine goodness. Historical Christian readings see here an announcement of the gathering of Jews and Gentiles in one people, but this should be understood as theological interpretation, not as an explicit statement of the text.

scholarViews.insight: The request for mercy and blessing upon Israel is linked to the desire that the name and way of God be known among the nations; God's goodness toward Israel affects its reputation among the peoples.
The psalm is understood as a public prayer for Israel's prosperity and the conversion of the Gentiles, pointing to a future in which Jews and Gentiles unite in praise.
The psalmist calls the nations to praise because God rules and judges rightly, so that the recognition of his righteousness leads the peoples to worship him.

questions: How can God's blessing on his life make his character visible to others?
Do you see praise to God as a response only to personal experience, or as a public testimony to the nations around you?
How does the conviction that God judges with equity changes the way you react to injustice and prosperity?
study.practice: Pray not only for personal needs, but for God to bless your home, your church and your people so that others know their salvation through their testimony. Also practice intentional praise: thank God for his righteousness, for his daily provision and for the universal scope of his kingdom. When you receive any material or spiritual good, turn it into the occasion of testimony, not self-reliance.
study.uncertainty: The biblical text provided does not accurately inform date, human author, historical occasion or place of composition. The possible reference to the post-exile mentioned by a commentator is a hypothesis, not textual certainty. Nor is it possible to affirm, only on the basis of psalm, that there is a direct and explicit reference to the Trinity; this is a later confessional reading present in part of the interpretative tradition.
